title: Chris King: How To Let Your Players Take The Wheel without crashing the car
speaker: Chris King
talk_title: How To Let Your Players Take The Wheel without crashing the car
description:
Hey! I'd love to talk about iterative game development and balance via community input, using examples from 30XX's time so far in Early Access (about a year and a half, so far. Not quite through yet!)

Vibe checking with our playerbase to identify fun points and pain points, maintaining groups of superfans that see some early early content even earlier, and open chats with our players have been instrumental components of 20XX and now 30XX's development, and I'd love to dig into some of our strategies for managing and acting on (or not acting on) fan feedback specifically in the context of replayable roguelites. My relationship with 20XX/30XX's players has been a major factor in both games' success, so I'm usually pretty excited to talk about it!

Lead-in music generated by Sonat Uzun.

segments.text: Next up we have Chris King developer/designer of
20XX and 30XX and co-cop friendly roguelike megaman-ish action platform games. Excellent.
CHRIS: Hi, everyone. My name is Chris King. I have spent the last 9-10 years making co-op
roguelike action platformers 20XX and 30XX and for so much of the game development cycles,
our relationship with our community and their input into our design iteration processes have
been such a critical component of us making these games that I thought I would take a little time
here to share about "How To Let Your Players Take The Wheel (without crashing the car)." One of the
advantages we have as roguelike is we have a natural audience that wants to play and replay
our games which means when we develop them open source fashion we have the same users respond
and get back with our feedback as we change things and we have the same audience that can
participate in this feedback ideation involvement. This is a quick talk about open development,
design iteration and community. This mass of players is the mass of players giving feedback
about your game every time you make a change. The actual size of the burbling mass might vary but
most of the principles are the same. If you are able to harness this player feedback correctively
and sustainablely I believe that leads to making better games. Two big reasons we care about player
feedback. The first is it is a really time efficient source of recognition and ideation.
Think of your game feature pipeline as having four components. Recognition being hey I realize I have
this system I would like to change. Ideation being it creative process you come up with ideation or
change proportionals. Decisions where you decide what subsets to implement to the game. For me, in
particular, I find that deciding from a wide pool of player ideated feedback gets pea to the point
where I can implement changes much faster than coming up with everything myself. I am a strong
proponent of open game development where you make the game live. We tend to be on Steam early access
for way longer periods of time than we originally think. Perspective sake is another reason. You
make a game for two years and you will never have any idea what your new player experience
is like. You will not know unless people tell you. Hopefully you went to make the game you
decided to make because you knew something great you wanted to player to experience ask you had a
great core concept but along the way you probably made a bunch of decisions that are flavor esthetic
clashes with some demographic of your would be player base. People find stuff about your
game that bugs them and they think sucks. Part of retaining a player base is not turning them off.
This short talk is about building your feedback firehose and drinking from it sustainably.
Everything is kind of to give folks hearing an initial nudge. I hope that you come away
from this if you are not already thinking about or integrating player feedback into your design
process you at least consider this. If you hear the couple of quick bullet point ways to build
that feedback and ways to deal with that feedback sustainably and all you think is that guy is full
of S and does wantant -- doesn't know what he is talking about that's wonderful. Maybe you hear
what I have to say and for you it is the opposite. That's fine. I am just hoping you think about it.
Getting players to give more feedback. It is difficult have to increase feedback and quality
can be challenging. You can certainly have them give you more which gives you more ideas
if you can process them all. The first one is to minimize friction like ned's ski suit here. You
want to make it as easy as possible for players to give feedback. Removing the barriers from the
players experiencing something they want to give feedback and being able to give the feedback. We
have a couple public forums, are active in Discord, use the Steam community and buttons
and links that link to our Discord community and Steam forums so if you have thoughts you can post
them. I want to but haven't had the time is I have seen a couple of games most recently
Rogue Legacy two had a button for most of early access where you could press F-10 and it would
automatically populate a form about diagnostic information that gives the developers context.
If that is feasible for you it is great. Remove as many barrier as you can think of from your
players being able to have a feedback in the experience. Maybe don't have players DM or
email you. It is time consuming for you. The other part is now that you have made it easy
for players to give you feedback, now encourage them to give you feedback by making it obvious
you care and are really listening. Players are more like to share their feedback with you if
they think you are actually paying attention. Would you call and tell someone, if you didn't
think somebody was listening, would you bother and call and say this I think this should be
different andical elevate the experience? Post in public spaces, chat in your Discord and be verbose
about patch notes and when you change stuff the players get to see the stuff you changed. If you
have community suggested changes that make it to the patch notes anybody reading can realize this
developer is taking this seriously. This gives you an opportunity to set the tone for your community
a little bit if you are civil and professional but not to you uptight about the way you interact some
of your community will follow your lead there. It gives them an opportunity to kind of be civil
and set a professional tone in how they deal with stuff. Those are two high level ways to
encourage players to give feedback. We move the barriers and encouraging them by getting them
to go you are listening and do care. A couple high level ways now to talk about interacting
with that increased volume of feedback without drowning in it. The worst thing that happens is
you encourage the feedback and don't develop a sustainable process for dealing with it and
burnout and say I haven't looked at my Discord in two weeks and it will take me two hours now
and that's obviously really tough. The first thing is interact efficiently. Encourage good
force multipliers. Good uses of your time. Where you can get your players to give you feedback in
public spaces. Discord is great even though it is ephemeral. Steam is great. Persistent forum
is wonderful because it let's everybody see your answers. When you discuss something about
your work in a public space more than just the questioner gets the answer if they chose to read
it and your veteran folks in the community are going to look at the answers you gave,
they are going to internalize those answers, and in the future they are going to give people those
answers for you so you don't have do it. In terms of your own scheduling and timing, any time you
have induced or incidental high tide, so patches, if your game takes off, releases, milestones,
any time you know the community is going to be especially active or if you have given them a
reason to be active, participate and be around. It is not free. It is expensive but cheaper than
coming up with the ideas and feedback yourself. During less busy times, batch feedback sections.
You may organically be able to figure it out yourself fall. I am checking out for the day
why don't I check with the community or I am on a break. You may hit points and this doesn't come
organically and if you realize this is happening schedule time for it. It can be overwhelming to
feel like I haven't responded to my fans in weeks and there is this big expectation. Going out of
your way to schedule it if you realize you are not doing it organically is really important.
Remember that obviously player feedback is incredible when it comes to general testing,
stability, that kind of bug and QA related stuff. There is obviously a lot of lesson there.
Here today specifically we are talking about the ideation and steps of feature design and
development. All of this still comes down to your taste. The important part I am trying to get at
is make sure as you comprehend and go through the wave of player feedback you receive that you are
still filtering it all through your own taste and experience. You are asking do the suggestions fit,
do they clash with other things, are they in work scope and that is the basis of another game,
obviously if a player is expressing a pain point or crash or this impacts my fun in the game these
are important. You are not instilling a democracy by doing this. You and your team are still the
sort of final arbiters of what goes into the work and what doesn't. Don't let hearing all
of the community feedback become I am just going to implement whatever is popular in the
community. It is not the way to go for us. We make sure that everything we are hearing from
the community -- we are actively listening and talking about things we agree or disagree with.
If there is popular stuff we are not going to do we will go out of our way to say we don't feel
like this is the right fit for the game but hear you are asking for it so the community knows we
are listening. On the other side of the coin lots of suggestions x from one-off suggestors. One user
I had never heard of before and never heard from again are really high and valuable for the game.
That's kind of everything I wanted to go through today. I know it is a lightning talk and all of
this is super-high level surface level stuff. But if you want to dig into this kind of thing
a little bit more, obviously, from a different perspective because it was three years ago,
I gave a talk about 20XX early access community development and interaction cycle a couple years
back. I wrote a long postmortem about 20XX after we finished it on now game developer. I am happy
to talk to anyone who wants to chat about it. As roguelike designers we have this wonderful
built-in community and we end up being able to retain individual players really well compared
to sort of the average game whatever that means and by harnessing that and letting players bepart
of the design recognition and ideation we can help ourselves back and make better games. I
think that's everything I have got. Thank you for listening. I hope this was informative or
giving you frame of reference for something. Thank you so much to the Roguelike Celebration
organizers and staff. It is fantastic seeing everybody's talk and I am looking forward to
checking it out the rest of the weekend. ALEXEI: You guys don't have to use your

Good job having a quick enough lightning talk. >> I planned for 10 minutes
knowing I would run over to 12. ALEXEI: Seeing no one has a question it is my
job now. I think you touched on it but maintaining the almost mental health boundary in terms of
being on and offline in terms of managing your -- how much you are drinking from the firehose.
Do you have any other quick tips for handling that aspect of taking in a lot of user feedback?
CHRIS: It is a wonderful question and the big and important thing comes up front and it is
planning. Planning for it. There is a slide I cut that was a chart of my personal community time on
20XX where I spent 8 hours a week interacting with the community. 15-16% of my total spent of
work time. If I had not made that time up front, if you don't plan for it, you don't have time to
do the job well. Just being able to, you know, it is obviously a very different form of work than
design than programming and whatever else you are doing that makes the game the game but it
is work just like anything else and if you don't treat it that way it is going to kick your butt.
ALEXEI: I am guilty. It is hard for a lot of us to know when to log off of
anything but especially your own game feedback. CHRIS: The only reason I know that is because I

ALEXEI: One super quick question. After a long early access, how do
you compartmentalize your committed players are no longer valid first time users either?
CHRIS: That's a wonderful question. You can't really. The feedback you get -- one of the things
you do as you interact with the community for several hours a week is you get to know people
and you can kind of understand their perspectives when they provide feedback and you sort of begin
to understand a little bit about the individual which also lets you sort of categorize their
feedback. This is kind of an offshoot of the question but I have at least one user in the
community that I know is pleasant and civil but is dooms day everything. If it his average level of
doom about a feature I intuitively understand this is average and his regular reaction to a
thing but as that happens you lose the ability to understand when somebody is new. Especially
when it comes to getting new player feedback, a lot of that bleeds over into alternative sources
of showing at conventions and specifically getting feedback related to demos if your
game is pre-release. That's very hard, though. It is a tough question to answer in just a minute.
